t: A Simple Trick That Makes Modeling Unforgettable ettable/
q: The way it works is that somewhere in the midst of your modeling exercise—regardless of what it is—you’re going to add an insignificant detail. That’s right. You’re going to add a step that has no purpose whatsoever.
The reason the strategy works is because it causes students to pay closer attention to you. It draws them into a visualization of the steps you want them to take.
If your students are able to see themselves completing the steps successfully, then that’s what they’ll do—no matter how challenging the task.

I had a small round target just below the inscription that each student would tap on their way in. It was a touchstone for them that would immediately shift their focus from life outside of the classroom to the expectations and responsibilities within.
It can be used simply as a small and simple way to get your students to sit up a little higher, smile a little broader, and engage a little deeper.
It will make your modeling more effective and your classroom more fun.
x: Adding a deliberately silly, purposeless step to modeling makes routines significantly more memorable for students.
The technique works because it draws heightened attention and strengthens students' visualization of the steps involved.
Visualization is central to effective modeling — students who can picture themselves succeeding are more likely to do so.
A physical touchstone, like a poster students tap, can transform a mundane transition into a meaningful ritual.

Linsin shares a specific modeling technique designed to make routines and expectations stick in students' memories: inserting a deliberately insignificant, silly step into an otherwise practical demonstration.

t: The Worst Cause Of Teacher Stress
q: The worst cause of teacher stress is trying to convince students to behave. It’s a reliance on your words to get them under control.
This approach to managing students manifests itself in the form of lectures, talking-tos, pep-talks, and threats. Intimidation and false praise are also telltale signs.
If relying on my wits and words were my primary way of curbing misbehavior, I’d find another profession. To smile through such burden day after day is agony.

The teacher’s responsibility is to teach great lessons, protect the rights of every student to learn and enjoy school, and create an environment they all look forward to. The student’s responsibility is to listen, learn, and behave according to the rules of the class.
Instead, follow the laws of the real world and let them experience the full weight of your consequences, all on their own and without cushioning their fall.
A grand piano will slide off your shoulders. Your smile will be real. And your students will thrive.

t: Why You Shouldn’t Send Students Out Of Class For Time-Out ss-for-time-out/
q: The biggest problem with out-of-class time-out is that your students will miss instruction time. Even if you send them with busywork or a reflection form , many will feel as if they got away with something.

For time-out to be effective, your students must feel like they’re missing something. When you send them out of your classroom this feeling is minimized because they’re unable to see what they’re no longer part of.
Another key to effective time-out is to wait until the student shows remorse before allowing them to return to their seat, which can only be done if they’re in the room with you.

Their willingness to follow this procedure , which must be taught and modeled in detail before putting into practice, is a reliable sign that they’ve reflected on their mistake and taken responsibility for it.
It must be a place that causes students to accept responsibility and vow not to make the same mistakes again.
Time-out, then, becomes not a break from the classroom or a shameful punishment, but an avenue through which your students can grow and mature and become better people.

t: How To Talk To Parents Who Just Don’t Care
q: But few don’t genuinely want what is best for their children. The key to talking to parents who don’t appear to care is to speak to that part of them that really, really does.
Whatever it takes to get the parent on the phone is worth doing. It can even be life changing.
The biggest key to tapping into that part of them that deeply cares about their child’s welfare is to speak to them as if they’ve been voted parent of the year.
This affectation of tone and expression is magic. Seldom have they been spoken to with such respect, and in response they’ll rise to meet the subtle call to be worthy of it.
Before hanging up, add the key line: “The reason I wanted to tell you personally is because I know you’d want to know .
Although it seems like a simple little thing, when you go out of your way to contact wayward parents in a non-judgmental way it almost always makes a profound difference.
x: His approach centers on speaking to the part of every parent that does genuinely want the best for their child.

Linsin pushes back on the notion that some parents simply don't care, arguing that the label is nearly always a misnomer masking uninvolvement, negligence, or personal struggle rather than true indifference.

t: How To Respond To An Angry Student
q: The worst mistake is trying to get to the bottom of it too soon. Asking why they’re upset almost always makes matters worse.
It’s best to wait until the angry student has forgotten the incident—sometimes hours later—before addressing the cause or enforcing a consequence.
Calmly pretending that nothing happened—or that what happened wasn’t a big deal—will take the attention off the student and release the tension in the room.
As for what to say, just let them know you’re giving them time and not making any judgments. Cruise by their desk and say, “No worries, Karla, I understand. We’ll take care of it later. I promise.
Like a first-responder who calmly surveys a chaotic scene, take a look around you first. Ensure the safety of the rest of your class before worrying about the angry student.
We’ve all been filled with anger and on the edge of losing our cool. And in those moments, what we need is not a lecture, not 20 questions, and not accountability.
x: Immediately investigating or disciplining an angry student almost always escalates rather than defuses the situation.
Teachers should first ensure the safety and calm of the rest of the class before addressing the angry student directly.
Brief, low-pressure reassurance that requires no response from the student can meaningfully calm them.
Linsin offers guidance for the difficult moment when a student becomes visibly, dangerously angry.
